notes.title: Anatomy of .gitlab-ci.yml
notes.gist: The file lists stages and jobs; each job is a named block with commands, and `default` sets shared values for every job.
points: Top-level global keywords: `stages`, `default`, `include`, `workflow`, `variables`.
Any other top-level key is a job; it needs `script` or `trigger`.
Reserved names like `image`, `services`, `cache`, `variables` cannot be job names.
`default:` sets `image`, `before_script`, `tags`, `retry` and more for all jobs.
A job's own value overrides `default`; `inherit:default: false` opts a job out.
notes.tip: Questions show a job without `image` and ask what runs: it inherits `default:image`. A job-level key always beats `default`, even for `tags`.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  F[.gitlab-ci.yml] --> G[Global keywords]
  F --> J[Jobs]
  G --> S[stages]
  G --> D[default: image, tags]
  G --> W[workflow, include]
  J --> SC[script or trigger]
  D -.->|inherited unless overridden| J

notes.title: Reuse config with extends and anchors
notes.gist: Write a job once as a hidden template, then let other jobs borrow it with `extends` or YAML anchors.
points: Hidden jobs start with a dot, like `.test-template`, and never run themselves.
`extends` deep-merges hash maps; keys set on the job itself take precedence.
`extends` can list several templates; supports 11 levels, keep it to three.
YAML anchors `&name`, `*name`, `<<: *name` only work inside one file.
`!reference [.job, script]` reuses one section, even across included files.
notes.tip: Merging never appends array items: if the job sets `script`, the template's `script` is gone. Anchors fail across `include` files; `extends` and `!reference` work.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  T[.base hidden job] -->|extends| A[job A]
  T -->|extends| B[job B]
  A --> M{Key on job too?}
  M -->|yes| J[job value wins]
  M -->|no| K[template value used]

notes.title: Pull in config with include
notes.gist: `include` stitches other YAML files into your pipeline, from your repo, another project, a URL, or GitLab's own templates.
points: `include:local` same repo; `include:project` plus `ref` for another project's file.
`include:remote` is a public URL; `include:template` is a GitLab-shipped template.
Files merge in listed order; later includes win, then the main file wins last.
Up to 150 includes per pipeline, nested ones counted; self-managed can change it.
`rules` is an array, so the top-level file's `rules` replaces the included one.
notes.tip: To override an included job, redefine only the changed keys in your own file; it merges last. Use `project` plus `ref` for pinned shared templates.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  L[include: local] --> MG[Merge in listed order]
  P[include: project + ref] --> MG
  R[include: remote URL] --> MG
  T[include: template] --> MG
  MG --> MF[Main file merged last, wins]
  MF --> PL[Final pipeline config]

notes.title: CI/CD components and the catalog
notes.gist: A component is a versioned, reusable pipeline piece with inputs, kept in its own project and shared through the CI/CD Catalog.
points: Add one with `include: component: <host>/<project>/<name>@<version>`.
Component files live in the project's `templates/` folder.
`spec:inputs` declares parameters; templates read them with `$[[ inputs.stage ]]`.
Version priority: commit SHA, then tag, then branch; `~latest` picks newest published.
Catalog releases must use semantic version tags like `1.0.0`.
notes.tip: If asked how to share tested, versioned config across many projects, components beat copy-paste includes. Pin a version; `~latest` can pull breaking changes.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  CP[Component project] --> TP[templates/ folder]
  TP --> SP[spec: inputs]
  CP -->|tagged release| CAT[CI/CD Catalog]
  CAT --> U[include: component, pinned version]
  U --> PL[Your pipeline jobs]

video.title: Monthly CI Updates: CI/CD Components Catalog

notes.title: workflow:rules gates the whole pipeline
notes.gist: `workflow:rules` is checked before any job and decides whether a pipeline is created at all for this event.
points: Rules are checked in order; the first match decides; no match means no pipeline.
Common gates: `$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"`, `$CI_COMMIT_TAG`, `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH`.
Use `$CI_OPEN_MERGE_REQUESTS` to stop duplicate branch plus MR pipelines.
`workflow:rules:variables` sets variables for the whole pipeline per condition.
`CI_MERGE_REQUEST_DRAFT` can skip pipelines for draft merge requests.
notes.tip: If a job allows tags but `workflow` blocks tag pipelines, the job never runs. Too-strict workflow rules can leave an MR stuck on Checking pipeline status.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  EV([Push, MR, tag, schedule]) --> W{workflow:rules match?}
  W -->|no| N([No pipeline created])
  W -->|yes| P[Pipeline created]
  P --> JR{Each job rules match?}
  JR -->|yes| J[Job added]
  JR -->|no| X([Job left out])

notes.title: Validate with CI Lint and editor
notes.gist: Check your YAML before pushing: the pipeline editor validates as you type and CI Lint can simulate a real pipeline.
points: Pipeline editor checks syntax live and shows the merged Full configuration.
CI Lint validates pasted YAML, including files pulled in with `include`.
Simulate pipeline creation for the default branch to catch `needs` and `rules` problems.
Also available through `glab ci lint`, the lint API and the VS Code extension.
notes.tip: Plain syntax check passes configs that still fail at creation, such as `needs` pointing at a rule-excluded job. Pick simulate when the question mentions logic errors.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  E[Edit in pipeline editor] --> V{Syntax valid?}
  V -->|no| FX[Fix YAML]
  V -->|yes| S[Simulate for default branch]
  S --> L{needs and rules OK?}
  L -->|no| FX
  L -->|yes| C[Commit and run]

summary.tests: Whether you can read and write a `.gitlab-ci.yml`: keyword placement, defaults, reuse with `extends` and `include`, and when a pipeline is created.
must_know: Global keywords: `stages`, `default`, `include`, `workflow`, `variables`; everything else is a job.
A job needs `script` or `trigger`; a leading dot makes it hidden, a template.
`extends` deep-merges hashes; the job's own keys win over the template's keys.
Arrays like `script` and `rules` are replaced on merge, never appended.
`include` types: `local`, `project`, `remote`, `template`, `component`; up to 150 includes.
`workflow:rules` decides if the whole pipeline is created, before any job rules.
Components are versioned: `@1.0.0`, `@~latest`; inputs read as `$[[ inputs.name ]]`.
traps: Thinking `extends` or `include` appends to `script`: the later array replaces the earlier one.
Using job `rules` to stop duplicate branch plus MR pipelines; that is a `workflow:rules` job.
Assuming a basic CI Lint pass catches `needs` and `rules` errors; simulation does that.

flowchart LR
  EV([push, MR, tag, schedule]) --> RULES{rules, workflow:rules}
  RULES -->|match| PIPE[Pipeline]

notes.title: Job rules: if, changes, exists
notes.gist: `rules` is a checklist read top to bottom; the first rule that matches decides if and how the job joins the pipeline.
points: `rules:if` tests variables, `rules:changes` tests changed files, `rules:exists` tests files present.
Clauses in one rule combine with AND; separate rules act like OR.
Matching rule can set `when`, `allow_failure`, `variables` and `needs`.
`rules:changes` is always true for new branches, tags and schedules; use `compare_to`.
`only/except` is deprecated; do not mix it with `rules` in one pipeline.
notes.tip: A last catch-all `- when: on_success` runs the job in all other cases; without it, unmatched events skip the job. Order matters: put `when: never` exclusions first.

source.title: Specify when jobs run with rules

notes.title: needs builds a DAG
notes.gist: `needs` lets a job start once the jobs it depends on finish, without waiting for the whole previous stage.
points: `needs: [build_a]` starts after `build_a` only, even if other build jobs still run.
`needs: []` starts the job at once; good for lint and scanners.
`needs:optional: true` avoids a creation error when the needed job is excluded by rules.
With `needs`, artifacts come only from listed jobs; `needs:artifacts: false` skips them.
Stages and `needs` can be mixed; view links with Job dependencies in the graph.
notes.tip: Error 'X does not exist in the pipeline' means rules removed the needed job: add `optional: true` or fix its rules. Avoid mixing `dependencies` with `needs`.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  BA[build A] --> TA[test A]
  BB[build B, slow] --> TB[test B]
  TA --> DA[deploy A]
  TB --> DB[deploy B]
  L[lint, needs empty] --> DA

source.title: Make jobs start earlier with needs

notes.title: Manual, delayed and allowed-to-fail jobs
notes.gist: Some jobs wait for a click, start after a delay, or may fail without stopping the pipeline; a few keywords control this.
points: `when: manual` outside `rules` defaults to `allow_failure: true`, so it never blocks.
`when: manual` inside `rules` defaults to `allow_failure: false`: a blocking manual job.
`when: delayed` with `start_in: 30 minutes` runs the job later.
`allow_failure: true` shows a warning but lets later stages continue.
Only users allowed to push or merge a protected branch can run its manual jobs.
notes.tip: Asked for a production gate that holds later stages until approved? Blocking manual job: `when: manual` with `allow_failure: false`. Optional manual jobs never hold the pipeline.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  M[when: manual] --> Q{allow failure?}
  Q -->|true| O[Optional: pipeline carries on]
  Q -->|false| B[Blocking: later stages wait]
  D[when: delayed + start in] --> T[Runs after timer]

notes.title: Parent-child and multi-project pipelines
notes.gist: A trigger job can start a separate downstream pipeline, either a child in the same project or a pipeline in another project.
points: Child: `trigger:include: path/child.yml`; same project, up to two levels deep.
Multi-project: `trigger:project: group/app` with optional `branch`; no nesting limit.
Default: trigger job passes once the downstream pipeline is created.
`trigger:strategy: mirror` or `depend` makes the trigger job reflect downstream status.
Dynamic child pipelines run YAML generated by an earlier job as an artifact.
notes.tip: Monorepo with per-service configs points to parent-child; another team's repo points to multi-project. Need the parent to fail when the child fails? Add `strategy`.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  P[Parent pipeline] --> T1[trigger: include child.yml]
  P --> T2[trigger: project other/app]
  T1 --> C[Child pipeline, same project]
  T2 --> MP[Pipeline in other project]
  C -.->|strategy: mirror| P

video.title: Parent-Child Pipelines feature demo

notes.title: MR pipelines, merged results, merge trains
notes.gist: Merge request pipelines test the branch, merged results test the branch merged with target, and merge trains queue those merges safely.
points: MR pipelines need rules matching `$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"`.
Plain MR pipelines test only the source branch, ignoring target branch changes.
Merged results pipelines test the would-be merge commit.
Merge trains queue MRs, each tested on top of the ones ahead.
Fork MR pipelines run in the fork, with the fork's variables and config.
notes.tip: Asked how to keep `main` green when many MRs merge at once: merge trains. Jobs with no MR rule do not appear in MR pipelines.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  MR([Merge request]) --> P1[MR pipeline: source only]
  MR --> P2[Merged results: source + target]
  P2 --> MT[Merge train queue]
  MT --> MN[Main stays green]

video.title: Keep the main branch always green with GitLab Merge Trains

notes.title: Environments, review apps, safe deploys
notes.gist: The `environment` keyword records where a job deploys, so GitLab tracks deployments, review apps and stop jobs per environment.
points: `environment:name` and `url` create the environment on first deploy.
Dynamic names like `review/$CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG` give one review app per branch.
`environment:on_stop` names a stop job using `environment:action: stop`.
`auto_stop_in` stops idle review apps; protected environments are never auto-stopped.
`resource_group: production` lets only one deploy job run at a time.
notes.tip: Two pipelines deploying to production at once? Answer `resource_group`, not `needs` or stages. Protected environments limit who may deploy, not when.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  D[deploy review job] -->|environment: review/slug| RA[Review app]
  RA -->|MR merged or auto stop| S[stop job, action: stop]
  P[deploy prod job] -->|resource group| PR[Production, one at a time]

video.title: Speed-run - Configuring Review Apps (website)

summary.tests: Whether you can control when jobs run and in what order, split work into downstream pipelines, and wire up merge request and deployment flows.
must_know: `rules` are checked in order; first match wins; no match means the job is skipped.
`when` options: `on_success` default, `manual`, `delayed` with `start_in`, `always`, `never`.
`needs` starts a job when its listed jobs finish; `needs: []` starts it immediately.
`trigger:include` makes a child pipeline; `trigger:project` makes a multi-project pipeline.
`strategy: mirror` or `depend` makes the trigger job wait for downstream status.
MR pipelines need rules matching `$CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE == "merge_request_event"`.
`environment:on_stop` plus `action: stop` cleans up review apps; `resource_group` serialises deploys.
traps: Picking `only/except` for new config; `rules` replaces it and mixing both causes surprises.
Expecting a trigger job to fail with its child; without `strategy` it passes once created.
Forgetting `when: manual` inside `rules` flips `allow_failure` to false, blocking the pipeline.

notes.title: CI, CD and pipeline building blocks
notes.gist: A pipeline is the assembly line a push starts: stages in order, jobs inside them, each job run by a runner.
points: Continuous integration: build and test every change automatically.
Continuous delivery: always releasable, deploy by a manual step; deployment: automatic to production.
Pipeline = stages; stage = jobs; job = `script` executed on a runner.
Pipeline types: branch, tag, MR, merged results, scheduled, parent-child, multi-project.
notes.tip: Delivery versus deployment is the classic pair: a manual production gate means continuous delivery. A job always needs a runner; the GitLab server does not run scripts.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  C([Commit push]) --> P[Pipeline]
  P --> S1[Stage build]
  S1 --> S2[Stage test]
  S2 --> S3[Stage deploy]
  S3 --> R[Each job runs on a runner]

video.title: GitLab CI/CD Pipeline Tutorial for Beginners

notes.title: Stages and job order
notes.gist: Stages set the order of work; every job in a stage must pass before the next stage starts, unless `needs` says otherwise.
points: No `stages:` defined means `.pre`, `build`, `test`, `deploy`, `.post`.
A job without `stage` goes to `test`.
`.pre` always runs first and `.post` always last, whatever the list order.
A failed job stops later stages unless it has `allow_failure: true`.
Same-stage jobs run in parallel if enough runners are free.
notes.tip: Watch for jobs with no `stage`: they land in `test`. Pipeline graph sorts jobs alphabetically, which is not run order.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  PRE[.pre] --> B[build]
  B --> T[test: default stage]
  T --> D[deploy]
  D --> POST[.post]
  T -.->|job fails| X([later stages stop])

notes.objective: CI/CD variables (predefined, custom, file-based, protected, masked)
notes.title: Where variables live and who wins
notes.gist: A variable can be set in many places; when names clash GitLab takes the most specific, most recent source.
points: Top: security policy variables, then manual job variables, then pipeline variables.
Pipeline variables come from Run pipeline, schedules, API, triggers and upstream pipelines.
Then project, group (closest subgroup wins), instance, then dotenv report variables.
YAML order: `rules:variables`, job `variables`, `workflow:rules:variables`, top-level `variables`.
Predefined variables rank lowest; keep secrets in UI settings, not YAML.
notes.tip: Project UI variable and job `variables:` share a name: the UI one wins. A value typed on Run pipeline beats both.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  A[Policy and manual job vars] --> B[Pipeline vars: UI, schedule, API]
  B --> C[Project, group, instance vars]
  C --> D[dotenv report vars]
  D --> E[YAML: rules, job, workflow, global]
  E --> F[Predefined vars, lowest]

notes.objective: CI/CD variables (predefined, custom, file-based, protected, masked)
notes.title: Protected, masked, hidden and file variables
notes.gist: UI variables carry flags that limit where a value is available and stop it showing in logs.
points: Protected: only pipelines on protected branches or tags receive the value.
Masked: shown as `[MASKED]`; value must be 8 or more characters.
Hidden: masked and never revealed in settings; only set when creating it.
File type: value saved to a temp file; the variable holds its path, e.g. kubeconfig.
Masking is not full protection; review `.gitlab-ci.yml` changes before running them.
notes.tip: Deploy works on `main` but fails on a feature branch with an empty token? The variable is protected. Masked does not mean protected.

notes.objective: CI/CD variables (predefined, custom, file-based, protected, masked)
notes.title: Predefined variables you will see
notes.gist: GitLab injects ready-made variables into every job that describe the commit, branch, pipeline and project.
points: `CI_PIPELINE_SOURCE`: `push`, `merge_request_event`, `schedule`, `web`, `trigger`, `pipeline`.
`CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` is unset in tag and MR pipelines; `CI_COMMIT_TAG` only in tag pipelines.
`CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG`: lowercase, URL-safe branch name for URLs and environment names.
`CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA` is the first 8 characters, handy for image tags.
`CI_JOB_TOKEN` is valid only while the job runs; `CI_DEFAULT_BRANCH` names main.
notes.tip: Rules testing `$CI_COMMIT_BRANCH` silently miss MR pipelines. For branch names with slashes in URLs or artifact names, pick `CI_COMMIT_REF_SLUG`.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  S{CI PIPELINE SOURCE} -->|push| BR[Branch or tag pipeline]
  S -->|merge request event| MR[MR pipeline]
  S -->|schedule| SC[Scheduled pipeline]
  S -->|web| WB[Run pipeline button]
  S -->|trigger or pipeline| DS[API or downstream]

notes.title: Artifacts pass results between jobs
notes.gist: Artifacts are files a job uploads to GitLab so later jobs, and people, can download them.
points: `artifacts:paths` picks files; `artifacts:expire_in: 1 week` sets how long they stay.
No `expire_in`: the instance default applies, 30 days out of the box.
Latest successful artifacts per ref are kept by default, whatever `expire_in` says.
Later jobs fetch all earlier-stage artifacts; `dependencies: []` or `needs` narrows this.
`artifacts:when: always` keeps logs from failed jobs; `artifacts:reports` feed MR widgets.
notes.tip: Output for a later stage of the same pipeline belongs in artifacts. Expect `dependencies` to list only earlier-stage jobs; same-stage needs `needs:artifacts`.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  B[build job] -->|artifacts: dist/| G[(Stored in GitLab)]
  G --> T[test job, later stage]
  G --> D[deploy job]
  G -->|expire in passed| X([Deleted])

video.title: Learn about GitLab Artifacts and Cache

notes.title: Cache speeds up repeat downloads
notes.gist: Cache keeps things like downloaded packages between runs so jobs skip reinstalling them; losing it must be harmless.
points: Cache is best effort and stored with the runner, or in S3 when distributed.
`cache:key` separates caches; `cache:key:files: [package-lock.json]` refreshes when the lockfile changes.
`cache:policy`: `pull-push` default, `pull` for read-only jobs, `push` to only save.
`fallback_keys` tries up to five other keys when the main key misses.
Protected and unprotected branches use separate caches by default.
notes.tip: Classic trap: cache vs artifacts. Dependencies reused across pipelines go in cache; build output needed downstream goes in artifacts. Many jobs reading one cache want `policy: pull`.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Q{What is the file?} -->|downloaded deps| C[cache: key, policy]
  Q -->|build output for later jobs| A[artifacts: paths]
  C --> R[Reused across pipelines, may miss]
  A --> S[Guaranteed in same pipeline]

notes.title: Services for databases in tests
notes.gist: `services` starts extra containers, like a database, next to the job container so tests can talk to them over the network.
points: `services: [postgres:16]` starts Postgres beside the job's `image`.
Reach it by hostname, `postgres`, not `localhost` or a socket.
`alias` sets a custom hostname; slashes in image names become `__`.
Configure the service with job variables, like `POSTGRES_PASSWORD`.
Needs a Docker or Kubernetes executor; shell executor ignores `services`.
notes.tip: Tests fail to connect to `localhost:5432`? Use the service hostname. `docker:dind` is also just a service, used to build images.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  J[Job container: image] -->|host: postgres| DB[(Service: postgres)]
  J -->|host: redis| RD[(Service: redis)]
  V[Job variables] -.-> DB

summary.tests: Core vocabulary and mechanics: stages and jobs, how variables are defined and ranked, and how artifacts, cache and services move data around.
must_know: Stages run in order, their jobs in parallel; defaults: `.pre`, build, test, deploy, `.post`.
Variable precedence, high to low: policy, manual job, pipeline, project, group, instance, YAML, predefined.
Protected variables reach only pipelines on protected branches or tags.
Masked values print as `[MASKED]`; they must be 8 or more characters.
Artifacts pass build output to later jobs; default expiry comes from instance settings, often 30 days.
Cache speeds up repeat downloads, is best effort, and lives with the runner.
Services run a sidecar container reached by its hostname, like `postgres`, not `localhost`.
traps: Using cache to pass build output to the deploy job; artifacts are the reliable way.
Expecting a protected variable on a feature branch; it is simply empty there.
Assuming `.gitlab-ci.yml` variables beat project UI variables; UI variables rank higher.

notes.title: Read logs and enable debug trace
notes.gist: Read the job log first; when it is not enough, debug tracing prints every command and variable.
points: Set `CI_DEBUG_TRACE: "true"` on one job, or as a pipeline variable, for full trace.
Debug logs can show secret values; restrict who can read job logs first.
Image pull errors like pull access denied usually mean registry auth or a wrong path.
Retry a failed job from its page; rerun a passed job to check flakiness.
notes.tip: Asked for the most detail on a failing script: `CI_DEBUG_TRACE`. The safe answer limits it to one job, because it can print masked secrets.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  F([Job failed]) --> L[Read job log]
  L --> Q{Cause clear?}
  Q -->|yes| FX[Fix and rerun]
  Q -->|no| D[Set debug trace on that job]
  D --> FX

notes.title: Pipeline or job did not appear
notes.gist: When a job or a whole pipeline is missing, the cause is almost always rules, workflow rules, or a broken `needs` link.
points: No pipeline at all: check `workflow:rules` and `[skip ci]` in the commit message.
Job missing: its `rules` had no match or matched `when: never`.
Two pipelines per push: branch and MR pipelines both ran; fix with `workflow:rules`.
Creation error on `needs`: the needed job was excluded; use `needs:optional`.
Check the merged result in the pipeline editor's Full configuration tab.
notes.tip: Duplicate pipelines are a `workflow:rules` problem, not a runner problem. Mixing `only/except` jobs with `rules` jobs is a common hidden cause.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  S([Something missing]) --> Q{Whole pipeline?}
  Q -->|yes| W[Check workflow rules, skip ci]
  Q -->|no| R[Check job rules order]
  R --> N{needs error?}
  N -->|yes| O[Add needs optional]
  N -->|no| L[Simulate in CI Lint]

notes.title: Stuck jobs, retries and timeouts
notes.gist: A job waiting forever lacks a matching runner; flaky jobs can retry; slow ones can be capped by a timeout.
points: Stuck pending: no online runner has all the job's `tags`, or untagged jobs are off.
`retry: 2` is the maximum; default is `0`.
`retry:when: [runner_system_failure, stuck_or_timeout_failure]` retries only infra failures.
`timeout: 3h` per job; may exceed project timeout, never the runner's timeout.
Protected-only runners skip jobs from unprotected branches, which then wait.
notes.tip: Retry is for infrastructure noise, not broken tests. A pending job with tags `[gpu]` means no available runner has the `gpu` tag.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  P([Job pending]) --> T{Runner with all tags online?}
  T -->|no| FIX[Add tag or runner]
  T -->|yes| RUN[Job runs]
  RUN --> F{Infra failure?}
  F -->|yes| RT[retry when, max 2]
  F -->|no| CODE[Fix the code]

notes.title: Run work in parallel and matrices
notes.gist: `parallel` copies one job so many runners share the work; `parallel:matrix` runs one copy per combination of values.
points: `parallel: 5` creates `test 1/5` to `test 5/5`; allowed values 1 to 200.
Each copy gets `CI_NODE_INDEX` and `CI_NODE_TOTAL` to pick its test slice.
`parallel:matrix` with lists of variables runs every combination, e.g. OS by version.
`needs` can point to specific matrix jobs.
Requires several runners or a runner with enough concurrency.
notes.tip: Split a slow test suite across machines: `parallel: N` plus `CI_NODE_INDEX`. Test several versions or platforms: `parallel:matrix`.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  J[test job, parallel: 3] --> A[test 1/3]
  J --> B[test 2/3]
  J --> C[test 3/3]
  M[parallel: matrix OS x version] --> M1[linux 20]
  M --> M2[windows 22]

video.title: Supercharge CI/CD with GitLab Matrix Builds: Test Across Platforms in Parallel!

notes.title: Make slow pipelines faster
notes.gist: Speed comes from running less, running earlier, and downloading less; GitLab has a keyword for each.
points: Fail fast: put lint and quick checks first, or `needs: []`.
`interruptible: true` cancels outdated jobs when a newer commit arrives.
`rules:changes` skips jobs for untouched parts of a monorepo.
`cache:key:files` reuses dependencies until the lockfile changes; `cache:when` caches even on failure.
Use small purpose-built images; set `expire_in` so old artifacts do not pile up.
notes.tip: Choose `interruptible` for wasted runs on superseded commits, `needs` for stage waiting, cache for slow installs. Bigger runners alone rarely is the intended answer.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  S([Slow pipeline]) --> W{Where is time lost?}
  W -->|waiting on stages| N[needs DAG]
  W -->|old commits running| I[interruptible]
  W -->|unneeded jobs| R[rules: changes]
  W -->|installs| C[cache key files]
  W -->|image pulls| IM[smaller images]

summary.tests: Whether you can work out why a job failed, did not run, or got stuck, and which keywords make a slow pipeline faster.
must_know: Start with the job log; `CI_DEBUG_TRACE: "true"` prints every command, and may expose secrets.
CI Lint simulation catches `needs` and `rules` errors before running.
Pending jobs usually mean no online runner has every tag the job lists.
`retry` allows 0 to 2 retries; `retry:when` limits it to failure types like `runner_system_failure`.
`parallel: N` splits one job N ways; `parallel:matrix` runs one job per variable combination.
`interruptible: true` lets newer pipelines cancel old redundant jobs.
`needs`, `rules:changes`, `cache:key:files` and small images cut runtime.
traps: Raising `retry` to fix a real test failure; retry suits flaky runner or network issues.
Enabling debug trace on a public project log, leaking variable values.
Thinking `parallel` needs no capacity; you still need enough runners or concurrency.

notes.title: Building Docker images in CI
notes.gist: To run `docker build` inside a job you need a Docker daemon: a dind service, the host's socket, or a shell runner.
points: Docker-in-Docker: `services: [docker:24-dind]`; runner must allow `privileged` mode.
Recommended TLS: `DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: "/certs"` with `/certs/client` shared.
No TLS: `DOCKER_HOST: tcp://docker:2375` and `DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: ""`.
Socket binding mounts `/var/run/docker.sock`; no privileged mode, but host-level access.
Daemonless alternative: Buildah builds OCI images without privileged Docker.
notes.tip: Error 'Cannot connect to the Docker daemon' usually means a missing dind service or privileged flag. Questions favour TLS-enabled dind as the secure default.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Q{Need docker build} --> DIND[dind service]
  Q --> SOCK[Socket binding]
  Q --> SH[Shell executor]
  Q --> BU[Buildah, no daemon]
  DIND -->|needs| PRIV[privileged runner]
  SOCK -->|risk| HOST[Shares host daemon]

source.title: Use Docker to build Docker images

notes.title: Push images to Container Registry
notes.gist: Every project can hold its own images; jobs log in with built-in variables and push tags based on the commit.
points: `docker login -u $CI_REGISTRY_USER -p $CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD $CI_REGISTRY`.
`$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE` is the project's registry path, e.g. `registry.example.com/group/app`.
`CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD` equals the job token and expires when the job ends.
Tag per commit, `$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA`; tag `latest` only from `main`.
Cleanup policies prune old tags to save storage.
notes.tip: Need long-lived registry access from outside a job, like a Kubernetes cluster? Use a deploy token, not `CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD`.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  B[build job] -->|docker login with CI vars| R[(Project registry)]
  B -->|push image:short sha| R
  R --> T[test job pulls image]
  R --> D[deploy job on main tags latest]

notes.title: Publish packages to Package Registry
notes.gist: GitLab can host your libraries in standard formats like npm, Maven, PyPI or generic files, published straight from a pipeline.
points: Formats include npm, Maven, PyPI, NuGet, Composer, Conan, Terraform and generic.
Pipelines authenticate with `CI_JOB_TOKEN`; outside CI use deploy or access tokens.
Generic packages store any file; up to 5 GB per file on GitLab.com.
Packages do not expire like artifacts; clean them up yourself.
notes.tip: Asked which credential a publish job uses: `CI_JOB_TOKEN`. For files kept beyond `expire_in` or shared across projects, prefer the package registry.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  J[publish job] -->|CI JOB TOKEN| PR[(Package registry)]
  PR --> N[npm]
  PR --> MV[Maven]
  PR --> PY[PyPI]
  PR --> GN[Generic files]
  PR --> C[Other projects install]

video.title: GitLab Single Project Package Registry Demo

notes.title: Dependency proxy avoids Docker Hub limits
notes.gist: The dependency proxy is a group-level pull-through cache for Docker Hub images, so repeat pulls skip Docker Hub's rate limits.
points: Enabled per group; admins can switch it on or off instance-wide.
Use `image: ${CI_DEPENDENCY_PROXY_GROUP_IMAGE_PREFIX}/node:20` in jobs.
Proxies Docker Hub images; cached copies use group storage.
Jobs can log in with `CI_DEPENDENCY_PROXY_USER` and `CI_DEPENDENCY_PROXY_PASSWORD`.
notes.tip: Pipeline fails with Docker Hub 'too many requests'? Answer: dependency proxy prefix. A registry mirror is the runner-admin alternative.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  J[CI job image] -->|group image prefix| DP[Dependency proxy]
  DP --> Q{Cached?}
  Q -->|yes| J2[Served from GitLab]
  Q -->|no| DH[(Docker Hub)]
  DH --> DP

video.title: Dependency Proxy for containers. GitLab v11.11

summary.tests: How a pipeline builds container images, logs in and pushes to GitLab's registries, publishes packages, and avoids Docker Hub limits.
must_know: Docker-in-Docker: `image: docker` plus `services: [docker:dind]`, runner in privileged mode.
TLS dind uses `DOCKER_TLS_CERTDIR: "/certs"`; empty value disables TLS on port 2375.
Socket binding avoids privileged mode but shares the host daemon, a security risk.
Log in with `$CI_REGISTRY_USER` and `$CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD` to `$CI_REGISTRY`.
Tag images `$CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE:$CI_COMMIT_SHORT_SHA`, not `latest` on every build.
Package registry jobs authenticate with `CI_JOB_TOKEN`.
Dependency proxy caches Docker Hub images: prefix with `$CI_DEPENDENCY_PROXY_GROUP_IMAGE_PREFIX`.
traps: Hard-coding a personal token for registry login when job variables already exist.
Expecting `CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD` to work after the job; it lives only while the job runs.
Treating the dependency proxy as a project feature; it is enabled per group.

domains.diagram:
flowchart LR
  MR([Merge request]) --> SAST[SAST]
  MR --> SEC[Secret detection]
  MR --> DS[Dependency scanning]

notes.title: Add SAST with a template
notes.gist: SAST reads your source code for security bugs; you switch it on by including GitLab's template and letting it pick analyzers.
points: `include: - template: Jobs/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml` adds the jobs.
Analyzers auto-detect languages; most run on Semgrep-based rules.
Jobs land in the `test` stage, which must exist in `stages`.
Output: `gl-sast-report.json` via `artifacts:reports:sast`.
Free tier gets the JSON report; MR findings and dashboards need Ultimate.
notes.tip: SAST scans source code, not running apps (DAST) or dependencies. Pipeline errors after adding SAST often mean `stages` no longer lists `test`.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  I[include SAST template] --> J[SAST jobs in test stage]
  J --> A{Language detected}
  A --> AN[Matching analyzer runs]
  AN --> R[gl-sast-report.json]
  R --> MR[MR widget, vulnerability report]

video.title: Add Security Scanning to your CI/CD pipeline in under 1 min

notes.title: Which scanner finds what
notes.gist: Each scanner looks at a different thing: your code, your packages, your images, leaked secrets, or the running app.
points: SAST: source code. Secret detection: committed keys and tokens.
Dependency scanning: known-vulnerable libraries from lockfiles like `requirements.txt`.
Container scanning: OS and package flaws in an image, via `Jobs/Container-Scanning.gitlab-ci.yml`.
Set `CS_IMAGE`; for other registries add `CS_REGISTRY_USER` and `CS_REGISTRY_PASSWORD`.
DAST: attacks a running app, often a review app.
notes.tip: Map the asset to the scanner: image means container scanning, lockfile means dependency scanning, password in git means secret detection.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  SRC[Source code] --> SAST[SAST]
  GIT[Commits] --> SD[Secret detection]
  LOCK[Lockfiles] --> DS[Dependency scanning]
  IMG[Container image] --> CS[Container scanning]
  APP[Running app] --> DAST[DAST]

video.title: How to set up Container Scanning using GitLab

notes.objective: Security scan results and vulnerability reports
notes.title: Reading scan results
notes.gist: Scanners write JSON report artifacts; GitLab reads them to show findings in the merge request and the vulnerability report.
points: Reports are declared with `artifacts:reports:*`, e.g. `sast`, `container_scanning`.
MR widget shows new findings versus the target branch.
Vulnerability report lists findings on the default branch for triage.
Scanner jobs use `allow_failure: true` so findings do not break the pipeline.
Use rules or policies, not job failure, to block risky merges.
notes.tip: If a custom scanner's results do not show in the MR, the job is missing the right `artifacts:reports` key. Plain `artifacts:paths` is not parsed.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  SC[Scanner job] -->|artifacts reports| RP[JSON report]
  RP --> W[MR security widget]
  RP --> VR[Vulnerability report]
  W --> AP{Approval needed?}

notes.title: Security policies enforce scans and approvals
notes.gist: Policies let a security team force scans into every pipeline and demand approval when findings appear, without editing each project.
points: Scan execution policy: runs chosen scans in pipelines or on a schedule.
Merge request approval policy: requires approvals based on scan results.
Pipeline execution policy: injects required CI/CD jobs into project pipelines.
Stored in a linked security policy project; `policy_scope` targets groups or projects.
Policy variables have the highest variable precedence.
notes.tip: Need scans in projects whose YAML you do not control? Scan execution policy. Need security sign-off on critical findings? Merge request approval policy.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  SP[Security policy project] --> SE[Scan execution policy]
  SP --> MA[MR approval policy]
  SP --> PE[Pipeline execution policy]
  SE --> P[Scans run in project pipelines]
  MA --> G[Merge needs security approval]

video.title: Creating security policies - The basics (HD)

notes.title: Code Quality reports in MRs
notes.gist: Code Quality shows maintainability issues from linters right in the merge request, read from a `codequality` report artifact.
points: Run any linter that outputs the Code Quality JSON format.
Declare it with `artifacts:reports:codequality`.
Old template `Code-Quality.gitlab-ci.yaml` uses CodeClimate; now deprecated.
MR report is on all tiers; pipeline report view needs Premium or higher.
Several tools can feed one pipeline's report.
notes.tip: Code Quality is about maintainability, not vulnerabilities. Findings missing from the MR usually mean no `codequality` report artifact.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  LT[Linter job] --> JS[Code Quality JSON]
  JS -->|artifacts reports codequality| MR[MR widget]
  JS --> PV[Pipeline report view]

video.title: GitLab Code Quality: Speed Run

summary.tests: Adding GitLab's security scanners with templates, knowing what each scans, where results show up, and how policies enforce scans and approvals.
must_know: Add scanners with `include: template:`, e.g. `Jobs/SAST.gitlab-ci.yml`.
SAST jobs run in the `test` stage; keep `test` if you redefine `stages`.
Container scanning uses Trivy; set `CS_IMAGE` to the image to scan.
Results come from `artifacts:reports`, like `sast` and `container_scanning` JSON files.
MR security widget and vulnerability report need Ultimate; the JSON report works on all tiers.
Scan execution policies force scans; MR approval policies require approval on findings.
Code Quality reads a `codequality` report and shows findings in the MR.
traps: Dropping the `test` stage when customising `stages`, so SAST jobs fail to load.
Picking SAST for vulnerable packages; that is dependency scanning.
Confusing scan execution policy with approval policy: one runs scans, one gates merges.

notes.title: Instance, group and project runners
notes.gist: A runner is the worker that runs jobs; its scope decides which projects can use it.
points: Instance runners serve every project; GitLab.com hosted runners are this type.
Group runners serve all projects in a group and its subgroups.
Project runners suit special hardware, credentials or isolation for one project.
GitLab Runner is a single Go binary for Linux, macOS and Windows.
Self-managed runners on GitLab.com should be kept on the latest version.
notes.tip: Shared across a team's projects without admin rights? Group runner. Special hardware or secrets for one repo? Project runner.
notes.diagram:
flowchart TB
  GL[(GitLab instance)] --> I[Instance runners: all projects]
  GL --> G[Group runners: group projects]
  GL --> P[Project runners: one project]
  I --> J[Pick up matching jobs]
  G --> J
  P --> J

notes.title: Choosing an executor
notes.gist: The executor decides where a job runs: a fresh container, the host shell, a Kubernetes pod, or a VM.
points: Docker: clean environment each job, supports `image` and `services`.
Shell: runs on the host as the runner user; no `image`, no clean environment.
Kubernetes: a new pod per job with build and service containers.
Docker Autoscaler and Instance executors scale with fleeting plugins.
SSH, Shell, VirtualBox, Parallels and Custom are in maintenance mode.
notes.tip: Need isolation and per-job images: Docker or Kubernetes. Questions with shell executors test that `image:` and `services:` are ignored.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  Q{Where should jobs run?} -->|fresh container| D[Docker]
  Q -->|existing cluster| K[Kubernetes]
  Q -->|on host directly| S[Shell]
  Q -->|autoscaled VMs| A[Docker Autoscaler]
  D --> IM[image, services work]
  S --> NO[image ignored]

video.title: Learn about the runner docker executor

notes.title: Install, register and config.toml
notes.gist: Install the runner on a separate machine, register it with a token, then tune it in `config.toml`.
points: Create the runner in GitLab first; it gives a `glrt-` authentication token.
`gitlab-runner register` asks URL, token, description, tags, executor.
`--non-interactive` with `--url`, `--token`, `--executor` scripts registration.
Settings save to `config.toml`; `concurrent` caps jobs across all runners there.
Registration tokens are deprecated; reuse one auth token across hosts for one config.
notes.tip: Want more jobs at once on one host? Raise `concurrent` in `config.toml`. Old answers with registration tokens are the deprecated path.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  C[Create runner in UI] --> T[glrt token]
  T --> R[gitlab-runner register]
  R --> CF[config.toml: executor, concurrent]
  CF --> RUN[Runner polls for jobs]

notes.title: Tags and protected runners route jobs
notes.gist: Tags match jobs to runners with the right abilities; protection keeps sensitive runners for protected branches only.
points: Job `tags: [gpu, linux]` needs a runner holding both tags.
Tags are case-sensitive; job `tags` replace `default:tags`, never merge.
Untagged jobs need a runner allowed to run untagged jobs.
`--access-level=ref_protected` makes a protected runner for protected refs only.
Jobs that share a cache should use tagged, consistent runners.
notes.tip: A job stuck pending with tags usually has no runner holding all of them. Protect deploy runners so feature-branch jobs cannot use production credentials.
notes.diagram:
flowchart LR
  J[Job tags: gpu, linux] --> M{Runner has all tags?}
  M -->|yes| R[Runs on that runner]
  M -->|no| P([Stays pending])
  PR[Protected runner] -->|only| PB[Protected branches]

summary.tests: Choosing runner scope and executor, registering a runner, and steering jobs to the right runner with tags and protection.
must_know: Runner scopes: instance (all projects), group, project; GitLab-hosted runners are instance runners.
Register with a `glrt-` runner authentication token; settings land in `config.toml`.
Docker executor: clean container per job, supports `image` and `services`.
Shell executor: runs on the host, no `image`, no isolation between jobs.
Kubernetes executor: a pod per job, build plus service containers.
A runner takes a job only if it has every tag the job lists.
Protected runners, `ref_protected`, run jobs only from protected branches and tags.
traps: Expecting `image:` to work on a shell executor; it is ignored there.
Thinking any one matching tag is enough; the runner needs all of the job's tags.
Using the deprecated registration token flow instead of a runner authentication token.
